opus-5.5.text:
I think a few things matter a lot, and some of them are a bit counterintuitive.

The first is a culture where people really care about the problem itself rather than about looking smart or publishing papers. Alignment is a strange field because the thing we most want to solve doesn't fully exist yet; we're trying to prepare for systems that are more capable than the ones we have. So you need people who are motivated by actually making the outcome go well, not by whatever metric happens to be easy to optimize in the short term.

Related to that, I think you want a strong empirical bent. It's very easy in alignment to spend a lot of time on abstract arguments about what future systems might do. Some of that is valuable, but I've become pretty convinced that the fastest progress comes from trying things on real models, seeing what breaks, and iterating. So I like a culture where someone says "I have an idea," and the natural response is "great, what's the smallest experiment that would tell us if it works?"

Another big one is being comfortable with being wrong and saying so openly. Many of our ideas won't work. If people feel they need to defend their research agenda at all costs, you end up with a lot of sunk cost and not much learning. Encouraging people to kill their own projects when the evidence isn't there, and treating that as a good outcome rather than a failure, is really important.

I also think collaboration matters more than people sometimes expect. A lot of alignment problems are big engineering problems as much as research problems. You need people who can build infrastructure, run large experiments, and write good evals, and those contributions need to be valued just as much as the clever new idea. If the culture only rewards the person with the conceptual insight, you won't get the work done.

And finally, there's a kind of seriousness combined with not being paralyzed. The stakes are high, and people should take that seriously, but you also want a team that's optimistic enough to actually try. If everyone thinks the problem is hopeless, they won't do the hard, grinding work that's needed. I'd describe the ideal as something like: clear-eyed about the risks, but genuinely believing we can make progress if we work hard and stay honest with ourselves.

r001.rationale: The response encourages admitting mistakes and abandoning unsupported projects, but it does not clearly say people should feel safe voicing controversial criticism of the team’s approach.

r002.rationale: It says the team should care about solving alignment rather than looking smart or publishing papers, and should prioritize making the outcome go well over short-term metrics.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, actually. The thing about alignment is that nobody really knows how to do it yet. We don't have a textbook, we don't have a mature field with established methods. So the first thing you need is a culture where it's okay to be wrong, and where people are actually trying to figure out what's true rather than trying to look smart or defend a position they staked out two years ago.

A big part of that is intellectual honesty. You need people who will say "I don't think this approach is going to work" even when it's the approach the team has been pursuing, and you need the team to actually welcome that rather than treat it as disloyalty. The failure mode I worry about most is a group that converges on one agenda and then stops seriously questioning it. Alignment is hard enough that you want a lot of disagreement, a lot of different bets being made, and then some real mechanism for updating when the evidence comes in.

The second thing is being empirical. There was a period where a lot of alignment thinking was very theoretical, and some of that was valuable, but I think the field made a lot more progress once we could actually run experiments on real models. So I want a culture that's hungry for contact with reality. Build the thing, test it, see where it breaks. Have the humility to let the models and the experiments tell you that your beautiful idea doesn't work.

Third, and this one is maybe underrated, is you need people who are genuinely motivated by the problem rather than by the prestige or the compensation or whatever. The timelines might be long, the work is often unglamorous, and a lot of what you do is going to turn out to be dead ends. If people are there because they actually care about getting this right, they'll stick through that. And it also matters for the harder situations, where there's pressure to ship something or to declare victory before you're really confident. You want people whose first instinct in that situation is to push back.

And then I'd say you need a mix of backgrounds. Alignment isn't just a machine learning problem. You want people who think like security researchers, people with a theory background, people who've done a lot of hands-on engineering, and people who are just really good at asking "wait, why do we believe that?" The best moments I've seen on teams are when someone from a totally different angle points out that the thing everyone assumed was obvious actually isn't.

The last thing I'd mention is that it has to be okay to work on things that are unfashionable or that won't produce a flashy result soon. A lot of the most important alignment work is going to look boring from the outside. Evaluation infrastructure, careful measurement, understanding failure modes in detail. If your culture only rewards the big exciting result, you'll systematically underinvest in exactly the stuff that makes the difference when it counts.

r001.rationale: The response says people should feel safe saying an approach will not work and that the team should welcome this rather than treat it as disloyalty.

r002.rationale: It prioritizes caring about solving the problem over prestige and compensation, but does not clearly address prioritizing alignment over securing individual credit for the work.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the most important things is having a culture where it’s easy to say, “I don’t know,” or, “I think we’re confused about this.” Alignment is a problem with a lot of uncertainty, and if people feel pressure to sound confident, you can end up hiding exactly the things you most need to investigate.

You also want people to be comfortable disagreeing, including with whoever is leading the team. If someone thinks our research direction doesn’t make sense, I want them to bring that up, and I want us to be able to discuss it without making it personal.

And then I think you need to balance that questioning with actually trying things. You can spend a very long time debating what alignment means or whether an approach could work in principle. Often the useful next step is to ask: what’s a small experiment we could run that would teach us something? Ideally, the team rewards finding out that an idea is wrong, because that’s progress too.

r001.rationale: The response says team members should feel comfortable challenging the research direction, including disagreeing with the leader, and discuss it without making it personal.

r002.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty, disagreement, and experimentation, but does not say the team should prioritize solving alignment over individual credit.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you want a culture where people are really trying to figure out what’s true, and where it’s easy to say, “I don’t know,” or, “I think our current approach has a serious problem.” Alignment involves a lot of uncertainty, so if people feel pressure to sound confident or defend whatever project they’re working on, you lose a lot of useful information.

That also means being able to disagree with the people leading the team. If someone junior notices something worrying, you want them to bring it up, and you want the response to be curiosity rather than defensiveness.

At the same time, you need to make concrete progress. You can spend a very long time discussing what alignment means without testing any of your assumptions. So I’d want a combination of careful thinking and a willingness to build things, run experiments, and change direction when the results don’t support your story.

And underlying all of that, I think the team needs a shared understanding that the goal is to make AI go well. Producing an impressive result is useful insofar as it helps with that goal.

r001.rationale: The response says people should be able to flag serious problems, disagree with team leaders, and raise worries without defensiveness, clearly supporting safe expression of criticism.

r002.rationale: It says impressive results matter insofar as they advance the goal of making AI go well, but does not address individual credit or prioritize alignment over claiming credit.
